summary: This experimental document describes Protocol Independent Multicast, Sparse Mode, a way to efficiently route multicast traffic to groups that may be spread across wide-area, inter-domain networks. It was replaced by RFC 2362.

eli5.summary: A magazine is sent only to the few homes that signed up, rather than to every house in town.

subtitle: Routing multicast traffic through the Internet for groups scattered across multiple networks.

tldr.problem: When one sender sends the same data to many receivers across the Internet, routers need to know where to forward copies, especially when group members are few and far apart.
tldr.mechanism: PIM-SM builds a shared distribution tree rooted at a Rendezvous Point, and routers join or prune this tree using Join/Prune messages to reach group members.
tldr.outcome: This made wide-area multicast efficient and independent of the underlying unicast routing protocol, but was later replaced by RFC 2362.

facts.label: Initial data path
facts.value: Encapsulated in Register messages to RP

today: RFC 2117 is marked Experimental and was replaced by RFC 2362, which refined the PIM-SM specification. PIM-SM became widely deployed as a standard way to handle multicast routing in sparse-mode networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2117 defines Protocol Independent Multicast, Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), a way for routers to forward multicast packets efficiently to groups whose members may be scattered across wide areas and even across multiple network domains. Traditional multicast assumes groups are dense (many members close together), but PIM-SM is designed for sparse groups where members are few and far apart, so sending to everyone would waste bandwidth.

The protocol is called protocol independent because it does not depend on which underlying unicast routing protocol the network uses. Whether routers run RIP, OSPF, or BGP, PIM-SM works the same way.
sections.eli5: This is a way for routers to send one message to many people without sending it to everyone. It works no matter what routing rules the routers already follow.

sections.title: The Shared and Source-Specific Trees
sections.content:
PIM-SM builds two kinds of distribution trees. First is a shared tree rooted at a central Rendezvous Point (RP) for each multicast group. All data to the group flows through the RP and then down to group members. This works immediately when a member joins.

Second is a source-specific shortest-path tree rooted at the actual sender. When data rates from a source are high, receivers can switch to this tree to get a shorter path and reduce latency. The router monitoring the group membership (the Designated Router, or DR) decides when the rate warrants a switch, usually after receiving many packets from a source.

A receiver first gets data via the shared tree, but can receive from both trees during a transition. This lets the protocol adapt: low-rate sources stay on the shared tree (saving overhead), while high-rate sources move to their own shortest paths.
sections.eli5: There are two routes: one goes through a central post office (the RP), and another is a shortcut straight to the sender. The receiver starts with the central route, but switches to the shortcut if the sender sends a lot of mail.

sections.title: Joining a Group and Sending Data
sections.content:
When a host wants to receive multicast for a group G, it tells its local router (the DR) using the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP). The DR looks up the RP for that group from a list called the RP-Set. It then sends a Join/Prune message toward the RP, with the group in the join list.

Each router on the path to the RP receives this message and creates a multicast route entry for the group, adding the downstream interface to its outgoing interface list. This builds the shared tree upward toward the RP.

When a sender sends data to group G, its DR initially encapsulates each packet in a Register message and sends it directly (unicast) to the RP. The RP decapsulates the packet and forwards it down the shared tree to all members. If the data rate stays low, this is efficient. If the rate is high, the RP can send Join/Prune messages back toward the source to switch to a source-specific shortest-path tree, and the sender then sends data natively (not encapsulated).
sections.eli5: A receiver sends a message saying "I want group G", and that message travels up to the RP, marking the path. When a sender starts, it sends packets wrapped up to the RP, which unwraps them and sends them down the tree. If a lot of packets come from one sender, the RP asks the sender to send them directly instead.

sections.title: Bootstrap Messages and RP Discovery
sections.content:
Each router needs to know which address is the RP for a given group. PIM-SM uses Bootstrap messages to distribute this information automatically within a domain. A domain is a contiguous set of routers running PIM and sharing a common boundary.

One router in the domain is elected as the Bootstrap Router (BSR) using a simple election mechanism: a set of routers advertise themselves as candidate BSRs, and the one with the highest IP address wins. A set of routers (usually including the BSR) also advertise as candidate RPs (C-RPs), sending their addresses and the groups they can serve to the BSR.

The BSR periodically creates Bootstrap messages containing the RP-Set (a list of C-RPs with their group prefixes) and sends them hop-by-hop throughout the domain. When a DR receives a membership indication or a data packet for a group with no matching route entry, it hashes the group address to select one of the RPs from the RP-Set, and sends Join/Prune or Register messages toward that RP.
sections.eli5: All routers in a region agree on one router (the BSR) to broadcast a list of post offices (RPs) that can handle each type of mail (group). When a router needs an RP, it uses a formula to pick one from the list.

sections.title: Multi-Access Networks and Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
When multiple routers are connected to the same physical network (like an Ethernet LAN), special mechanisms are needed to prevent duplicate packets. One router must be chosen as the Designated Router (DR) for the LAN, responsible for sending Join/Prune and Register messages on behalf of the LAN.

The DR is elected by Hello message exchange: neighboring routers send periodic Hello messages, and the router with the highest IP address becomes the DR. If a duplicate packet arrives on an outgoing interface (which should not happen), the routers use Assert messages to resolve which one should forward. The Assert message includes the metric and metric preference to reach the source or RP. The router with the smallest metric (using metric preference as a tie-breaker, with the highest IP address as a final tie-breaker) becomes the forwarder, and the others prune the interface from their outgoing lists.

PIM-SM also provides optional Join/Prune suppression on multi-access networks: if a router sees a Join/Prune message from another router with a longer hold time, it can suppress its own message temporarily to reduce overhead.
sections.eli5: When many routers are on one LAN, they vote on who sends the join messages (the one with the highest address wins). If a packet comes back from the wrong direction, they argue about it using Assert messages, and the one with the shorter path wins.
